Central Limit Theorem: sample means are approximately normal for large n, even if population isn't normal. This justifies using normal distribution for inference.
CLT says all data are normally distributed if you take enough samples.
Larger sample size decreases SE because SE = σ/√n. Larger n increases √n, decreasing SE, giving more precise estimates.
Standard error is the same as standard deviation and doesn't change with n.
Higher confidence level requires wider interval (larger z*). Trade-off: more confidence = less precision. Formula: Width = 2z*(σ/√n).
Wider confidence intervals have less confidence because they cover a bigger range.
Power = 1 - β = 1 - 0.10 = 0.90. This means 90% probability of correctly rejecting false null hypothesis.
Power = α = 0.05, the Type I error rate.
Residuals show random scatter around y=0 with roughly constant variance. No curved pattern, suggesting linearity is appropriate. Model seems adequate.
Curved residuals mean the model is perfect because it shows a smooth pattern.
A biased but lower-variance estimator can be preferable if it has smaller mean squared error than unbiased but higher-variance alternatives. Trade precision for accuracy.
Always use unbiased estimators regardless of variance.
One-sided: tests if parameter is greater/less than value (H₁: μ > 0). Two-sided: tests if different (H₁: μ ≠ 0). Use one-sided when direction is specified; two-sided for general differences.
One-sided and two-sided tests give the same answer; the names just describe how you state the hypothesis.
90% CI has z*=1.645. 90% CI is (40,50), width=10. To halve width to 5, need z*=0.822, which corresponds to ~67% confidence.
To reduce width by half, use half the confidence level: 90%/2 = 45% confidence.

Use median. Right-skewed distribution has mean pulled toward high tail. Median resists skewness and outliers, better representing central tendency.

Random sampling: each unit equally likely, more representative. Convenience sampling: selects available units, biased. Different methods produce different variability levels.
All sampling methods produce the same variability.
